title: Apply a multi-step vCenter VM change and report exactly which steps landed
prompt:
Platform automation ticket for our VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 estate. Build a Python package `vcfvm` at the workspace root, runnable as `python3 -m vcfvm`. It applies a multi-step change to one virtual machine through the vSphere Automation API for vCenter and reports, step by step, exactly which parts of that change landed on the endpoint.

Use the Python standard library only: `urllib.request` is the transport. Do not take a third-party HTTP or VMware dependency (`requests`, `httpx`, `pyvmomi`, `vsphere-automation-sdk`), do not vendor one, and do not shell out to `curl`.

The protected `docs/contract.json` is a projection of `specifications/vsphere/openapi/automation/vcenter.yaml` in VMware's Apache-2.0 `vmware/vcf-api-specs` repository at tag `9.0.0.0`, at the commit recorded in `docs/official_sources.json`. It comes from the specification, not from a documentation page, and not from the 9.1 revision of that same file. It names the only seven operations in scope, `Cis.Session_create`, `Vcenter.Vm.Power_get`, `Vcenter.Vm.Hardware.Memory_update`, `Vcenter.Vm.Hardware.Disk_create`, `Vcenter.Vm.Hardware.Ethernet_create`, `Vcenter.Vm.Power_start` and `Cis.Session_delete`, and for each one it carries the server base path, method, path template, pinned query string, security scheme, success status and request and response schemas. Take every property name, type and value set from that file. The acceptance harness may point `--contract` at a copy that serves the same operations under a different server base path, so resolve each request from the contract instead of hard-coding URLs.

Command line:

`python3 -m vcfvm --base-url <url> --username <user> --password <pass> --vm <moid> --report <path> --memory-mib <int> --disk-capacity-gib <int> --nic-network <moid> [--contract <path>] [--hot-add-enabled] [--disk-name <name>] [--disk-scsi-bus <int>] [--disk-scsi-unit <int>] [--nic-type <type>] [--nic-start-connected]`

`--contract` defaults to `docs/contract.json`.

Requirements:

- Authenticate once with `Cis.Session_create` over HTTP Basic, keep the session identifier it returns, and send that identifier in the `vmware-api-session-id` header on every later call. Those later calls carry no `Authorization` header, and the session creation carries no session header. Release the session with `Cis.Session_delete` on every exit path, including the one where the change failed.
- Run five steps in this order and stop at the first failure: `power_state` reads the current power state, `memory` resizes memory, `disk` attaches a newly created virtual disk, `nic` attaches a virtual Ethernet adapter, `power_on` powers the virtual machine on. Never retry a step and never continue past a failed one.
- `--memory-mib` is the new memory size in mebibytes. `--hot-add-enabled` turns on the flag that allows memory to be added while the machine runs.
- The disk step always creates a new VMDK backing and never attaches an existing one. `--disk-capacity-gib` is that backing's capacity in GiB, and the contract's capacity property is in bytes. `--disk-name` is the base name of the VMDK file. `--disk-scsi-bus` attaches the disk at that bus of a virtual SCSI adapter and also pins the host bus adapter type to SCSI; `--disk-scsi-unit` pins the unit number on that bus.
- The NIC step attaches the adapter to the vSphere standard portgroup network identified by `--nic-network`. `--nic-type` is the adapter emulation type, and `--nic-start-connected` asks for the adapter to be connected whenever the machine powers on.
- Every optional property the caller did not ask for must be absent from the JSON request body rather than sent as null, false or an empty object, and only an operation whose contract entry declares a request body may carry one. `Content-Type: application/json` belongs on the requests that do carry a body and nowhere else.
- `--report` receives a JSON object with exactly the keys `vm`, `outcome` and `steps`. `outcome` is `succeeded` when every step succeeded and `failed` otherwise. `steps` lists all five steps in the order above, each an object with `name`, `operation_id` and `status`, where `status` is `succeeded`, `failed` or `not_attempted`.
- A step that succeeded also carries `result`: `{"state": <power state>}` for `power_state` and for `power_on`, `{"memory_mib": <int>}` for `memory`, `{"disk": <identifier>}` for `disk` and `{"nic": <identifier>}` for `nic`, using the identifier the endpoint returned rather than one you chose. The step that failed instead carries `error` with exactly `http_status`, `error_type` and `message`, read out of the endpoint's own response: the HTTP status, the vAPI error discriminator, and the default text of the first localizable message. Do not reword it. A step that never ran carries neither `result` nor `error`.
- Exit 0 when the outcome succeeded and 1 when it failed, and write the report on both paths. Never print or store the password.

Acceptance: `python3 verify.py`. It boots a contract-pinned loopback vCenter on `127.0.0.1` with dummy credentials, drives the CLI through a change that fails at power-on, one that fails before any hardware change is submitted, and one that completes cleanly, then reads the mock's request log to assert the exact method, target, query string, authorization, JSON body property set and the omission of every unset optional property. No live VMware endpoint is contacted. `verify.py`, `mock_vcenter.py`, `.gitignore` and everything under `docs/` are protected; do not modify them.
